answers.java_tx_design: Over ten years, mostly at Kestrel Remit, I've owned transaction boundaries across three different services -- the one that still sticks with me is our cross-border transfer engine, handling something like 40,000 remittances a day at peak, mostly USD-to-PHP and USD-to-MXN corridors. Early on, the boundary wrapped the full transfer: debit the sender, call the FX-rate lock, call the payout-partner API, all in one transaction. Under partner-API latency spikes -- sometimes 8-10 seconds during their maintenance windows -- that held row locks on the sender's balance long enough to cause contention across unrelated transfers to the same corridor. I split it into three phases: debit-and-hold commits first, FX lock happens as its own step, and payout dispatch happens last, each with its own compensating reversal path. The first version of the FX-lock step had a gap -- if the lock expired before payout dispatch ran, we'd occasionally lock a rate twice for the same transfer under retry, which we only found after a customer complained about being charged two different rates for one transfer. That taught me to make every phase explicitly idempotent against retry, not just the whole transaction.
answers.java_ops: About four years ago, our transfer-dispatch service started getting OOMKilled on Kubernetes roughly four to five times a week during evening peak -- 6pm to 9pm Pacific, when both US and Latin American traffic overlap. GC logs showed G1 doing full collections every couple of minutes under load; heap was 4GB against a workload generating large temporary objects for every FX-rate lookup. I redesigned the rate-lookup path to reuse a shared, immutable snapshot object instead of allocating a fresh one per request, bumped heap to 8GB, and separately found our connection pool capped at 20 against a workload that needed closer to 60 during peak. p99 on transfer dispatch went from about 3.8 seconds to under 500ms, and OOMKills dropped to zero over the following six weeks. I tried horizontal scaling first, adding three more pods -- it helped throughput a little but didn't touch the pause-time problem, since each pod still hit the same per-object allocation issue.
answers.rust_readiness: I don't have production Rust experience, but I've been seriously working toward it for the last several months -- I finished the official book, built a small command-line tool that parses our FX-rate feed format as practice, and I'm now reading through the tokio documentation since our transfer-dispatch service is heavily async. My realistic estimate is another two to three months of side projects before I'd trust myself on anything production-facing, and I'd want to pair with someone who has shipped Rust before on the first real piece. On migration, given ten years of watching what happens when a team gets excited and rewrites too much at once, I'd want to pick the narrowest, most measurable piece -- probably the FX-rate lock service, since it's CPU-bound and has a clean boundary -- and run it alongside the Java version in shadow for at least a full settlement cycle before trusting it.
answers.rust_boundary: If I were moving part of our transfer ledger write path to Rust, I'd start with the FX-rate lock step I mentioned -- narrow, stateless between calls, no direct database ownership needed since it just returns a locked rate and an expiry. I'd keep the boundary as an internal gRPC call from the Java dispatch service, with the Rust service owning nothing but the lock logic itself, and the actual ledger write staying in Java. Before and after, I'd measure lock-acquisition latency, memory per instance, and -- critically for this specific piece -- the rate of double-locks under retry, since that's the exact failure mode I described earlier. I'd want at least a full settlement cycle of shadow traffic, comparing Rust's decisions against the Java path's decisions on the same requests, before cutting over anything live.
answers.money_correctness: At Kestrel Remit, every transfer request carries an idempotency key generated client-side, stored in Postgres with a unique constraint, and every retry from our own dispatch logic reuses that same key rather than generating a new one. About three years ago, a partner-API integration for a new corridor had a bug where their webhook confirming payout could fire twice for the same transfer under certain network conditions -- over about five weeks we found 340 transfers out of roughly 1.4 million processed in that window where we'd logged two confirmation events, though the unique constraint on our payout-confirmation table meant zero duplicate payouts actually went out. What it did expose was that our alerting only fired on payment attempts, not confirmation duplicates, so we were blind to it for those five weeks. We added a separate alert on duplicate confirmation events and fixed the partner-side webhook handling to dedupe by their event ID before processing.
answers.incident_response: The duplicate-confirmation issue I just described is the clearest incident I've owned start to finish. I found the pattern myself while investigating an unrelated support ticket, not through an alert, which was the actual gap we fixed afterward. I told my engineering lead within thirty minutes of confirming it wasn't a one-off, and we had the dedupe fix and the new alert deployed within three days, then spent the following week manually verifying all 340 flagged transfers against the partner's own settlement report to be sure no double payout had slipped through -- none had. The postmortem's main change was that new confirmation-duplicate alert; about a year later, a different partner integration hit a similar webhook-duplication bug, and that alert caught it within twenty minutes instead of five weeks.
answers.process_skipping: During the duplicate-confirmation incident, I wanted to skip our second-reviewer requirement to ship the dedupe fix faster, since I was confident in the change. I didn't -- I asked another senior engineer for a focused twenty-minute review instead of our usual next-day cycle, explained why it was urgent, and they caught that my dedupe key didn't account for one of the partner's older event formats still in use for legacy corridors. Outside a live incident like that, I've never skipped review or the deploy procedure in ten years, and on a system moving people's remittances to family members abroad, I don't think any amount of speed is worth getting that wrong.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: Early in my time at Kestrel, I shipped a config change that silently disabled retry on a non-critical notification queue -- not the transfer path itself, but customer-facing SMS confirmations. I noticed it myself the next day when delivery-rate metrics looked off, and told my manager within the hour, before any customer had complained. I've been on the transfer-platform on-call rotation for about eight years now, roughly one week in five, and I still take escalations from our support team when a customer disputes a transfer status. I've mentored six or seven engineers over the years, several of whom are now senior themselves, mostly around how to read our reconciliation reports and think about failure modes in payment systems.
answers.evidence_decision: About five years ago, a teammate wanted to move our FX-rate caching from a short TTL to a much longer one to cut load on the rate-provider API. I was against it, since rates in some corridors move fast enough that a stale cached rate could mean quoting a customer the wrong amount. I ran an analysis of actual rate volatility across our top corridors over a month, showing that for two of our highest-volume corridors, rates moved enough within a typical cache window to matter for larger transfers. The team agreed to a tiered TTL instead -- longer for stable corridors, short for volatile ones -- which is still roughly the design running today. I didn't get the outcome I originally wanted, uniformly short TTLs everywhere, but the tiered approach the team landed on was better than either of our starting positions.
answers.own_contribution: In the transaction-boundary story I described earlier, splitting the transfer into debit-hold, FX-lock, and payout-dispatch phases was my design -- I proposed it, built the first two phases myself, and wrote the compensating-reversal logic. The payout-dispatch phase itself was built by a teammate in parallel, following the interface I'd designed, and the specific retry-count and backoff numbers for that phase came out of a discussion between the two of us rather than my call alone -- he'd operated a similar dispatch system before and had good instincts on that part that I didn't.
answers.java_recovery: A different incident from the duplicate-confirmation one: a batch reconciliation job that reconciles our ledger against partner settlement reports crashed partway through one night, leaving about 900 transfers out of roughly 50,000 processed that night unreconciled -- not wrong, just not yet checked. I found the gap by comparing the count of reconciliation records written against our expected transfer count for that batch window, wrote a resume script that picked up from the last successfully reconciled transfer ID rather than restarting the whole batch, and verified it by confirming the final reconciliation count matched the transfer count exactly the next morning. An earlier incident, about six years ago, was worse -- a bug in an older version of this same job double-counted about 1,200 transfers as reconciled when they weren't, which I only caught because a partner's monthly settlement total didn't match ours; that one took nearly two weeks to fully unwind because I had to rebuild the correct reconciliation state from raw transfer logs rather than trusting the job's own output.
answers.java_perf_change: Beyond the GC work I mentioned, a separate performance project: our transfer-status API, which customers poll to check on a pending remittance, was sitting at p99 around 2.2 seconds under peak load, mostly from a query joining across four tables for every status check. I denormalized a status-summary table updated on write instead of computed on read, which took p99 down to about 180ms, measured over two weeks of production traffic. Before landing on that, I tried adding a Redis cache in front of the existing query instead -- it helped the average case but did almost nothing for p99, since cache misses during peak, a new transfer being checked for the first time, were exactly the slow case that mattered most to customers anxious about their money.
answers.rust_hands_on: I've only written the small CLI tool I mentioned -- a parser for our FX-rate feed format, built as a personal exercise, not production. The place I actually got stuck was trying to hold a reference to a parsed rate record across an async boundary while also mutating a shared cache of recent rates; the borrow checker wouldn't let me do both at once. I ended up restructuring it so the parsing step returns owned data instead of borrowed references, and the cache update happens as a separate step after, rather than trying to do both inside one async block. It's a small thing, but it's the first time ownership actually clicked for me instead of just reading about it.
answers.rust_when_not: I've held back full rewrites plenty of times in ten years, though not with Rust specifically yet. About four years ago there was real momentum on the team to rewrite our entire transfer-dispatch service on a newer internal framework, and I argued against it -- that service had years of corridor-specific edge cases baked into it, things like specific holiday calendars for different countries' banking systems, that weren't documented anywhere except in the code itself. We migrated one low-risk corridor first, measured it for about two months, and decided the risk on the rest wasn't worth it given how thin the actual performance gain turned out to be. I'd apply the same test to any Rust candidate: how often does the piece change, how well are its edge cases understood, and can we verify a rewrite against the old behavior before cutting over anything live.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: About two years ago, our monthly reconciliation against one partner's settlement report showed a mismatch of around $4,200 on a total settlement volume in the tens of millions -- small relative to volume, but it shouldn't have been there. I traced it to a batch of transfers that had been refunded by the partner after our reconciliation window closed for that month but before the partner's own report cutoff, a timing mismatch between when we considered a period closed and when they did. It affected about 60 transfers across that one partner relationship. We corrected it with new adjusting entries for each affected transfer rather than editing the original closed records, and moved our reconciliation window to run three days later in the month to give late refunds time to settle before we closed the books. My first theory was a currency-conversion rounding issue, which I ruled out once the mismatch amount didn't scale with transfer volume the way a rounding error would.
answers.prod_data_verification: I've been tempted plenty of times over ten years -- there was a point during the duplicate-confirmation investigation where querying live transfer amounts directly would have been the fastest way to confirm my theory. I didn't; we keep a daily-refreshed masked copy of the ledger with customer names and account numbers scrubbed but amounts, timestamps, and corridors intact, and I ran my diagnostics against that. For things that genuinely can't be reproduced off production -- like a partner-specific webhook timing issue -- our practice is a read-only shadow comparison against live traffic, reviewed by a second engineer before it runs, and announced in our incident channel beforehand so anyone watching dashboards knows why there's unusual read traffic. I've used that maybe five or six times over the years, always for exactly that kind of case.
